title: DAVID’S SON TURNED SEX INTO A PUBLIC DECLARATION OF REBELLION
paragraphs:
DAVID’S SON TURNED SEX INTO A PUBLIC DECLARATION OF REBELLION
Absalom did not climb onto that rooftop because he lost control of his lust. He went there to send a message to his father, to Israel, and to heaven: “David’s throne is mine now.” But the darkest scandal in David’s house was already exposing something terrifying about sin—and something breathtaking about the grace of Jesus Christ.
There are sins committed in darkness because the sinner desperately hopes no one will ever know.
Then there are sins committed where everybody can see because being seen is the entire point.
Absalom chose the second kind.
Picture Jerusalem.
David—the warrior king who once stood before Goliath, the shepherd who wrote songs of worship, the man God had lifted from obscurity to a throne—is fleeing his own capital.
Not because a foreign army has broken through the gates.
Not because the Philistines have returned.
His own son has turned against him.
And while David is leaving Jerusalem humiliated, barefoot and weeping, Absalom is entering the city as though the kingdom already belongs to him.
Then comes one of the most disturbing moments in David’s story.
Ahithophel, Absalom’s counselor, gives him advice designed to make reconciliation with his father politically unthinkable:
“Go in unto thy father's concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father: then shall the hands of all that are with thee be strong.”
—2 Samuel 16:21, KJV
And Absalom does it.
Not secretly.
Not somewhere behind a locked palace door.
A tent is erected on the roof.
The biblical narrator then delivers the horrifying sentence with almost unbearable restraint:
“So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.”
—2 Samuel 16:22, KJV
“In the sight of all Israel.”
That detail changes everything.
This was sexual sin, certainly—but it was also political theater.
Absalom was weaponizing sex as a public declaration of rebellion.

The women were caught inside a power struggle they did not create. Scripture later tells us that David provided for these ten women but separated them from ordinary marital life, and they remained in confinement “living in widowhood” until their deaths. Their suffering should not disappear merely because kings and princes dominate the narrative. Powerful men made decisions, and women lived with the consequences. See 2 Samuel 20:3.
But to understand just how outrageous Absalom’s action was, listen to the language of the Torah.
Leviticus 18:8 says:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה עֶרְוַת אָבִיךָ הִוא
“‘Ervat eshet-avikha lo tegalleh; ‘ervat avikha hi.”
Literally, the sense is:
“The nakedness of your father’s wife you shall not uncover; it is your father’s nakedness.”

The Hebrew word עֶרְוָה—‘ervah—carries the idea of nakedness or exposed nakedness, and in this legal context “uncovering nakedness” functions as sexual language. The command is not ambiguous. Sexual relations with one’s father’s wife violated a boundary God had explicitly established.
Absalom did not merely cross a social line.
He trampled a divine boundary.
And he did it publicly.
He turned what God had forbidden into a political announcement.
The message was unmistakable:
My father is finished.
His household is mine.
His royal privileges are mine.
His authority is mine.
His throne will be mine.
There would be no quiet reconciliation after this.
That was precisely the strategy.
Ahithophel wanted all Israel to hear what Absalom had done so that Absalom’s supporters would understand that the rupture between father and son had become irreversible.
This is what rebellion eventually does.
At first, rebellion whispers.
Later, it demands a microphone.
At first, sin wants a hidden room.
Eventually, if continually fed, it can begin demanding the rooftop.
And before we point at Absalom with too much confidence, there is something painfully familiar here.
Maybe your rebellion never involved a palace.
Maybe nobody erected a tent.
Maybe thousands of people never watched your worst decision.
But rebellion does not require a crown.
Sometimes rebellion sounds like:
“God, I know what You said…but I want this.”
“I know this relationship is pulling me away from Christ…but I don't want to surrender it.”
“I know I should forgive…but I want them to suffer.”
“I know nobody knows what I watch when I am alone.”
“I know what I keep deleting.”
“I know what I keep hiding.”
“I know this bitterness is poisoning me.”
“I know this compromise is becoming normal.”
“I know I have learned how to look Christian while protecting something from Christ.”
That is where this story stops being ancient history.
Because there may be a little rooftop inside every human heart.
A place where we want the throne.
A place where we tell God, perhaps without saying the words:
This part belongs to me.
You may have my Sundays.
You may have my worship songs.
You may have the Bible sitting beside my bed.
You may have the Christian language I use around Christian people.
But You cannot have this.
And Jesus does not come merely to negotiate visitation rights over the rooms of your heart.
He is Lord.
That is why the Gospel is simultaneously terrifying to our pride and beautiful to our souls.
Christ does not merely offer to improve the kingdom you have built around yourself.
He calls you to surrender the throne.
But there is another layer to Absalom’s rooftop that makes this story even more sobering.
Years earlier, David had committed his own sexual sin.
He took Bathsheba and then arranged circumstances that led to the death of her husband, Uriah.
David tried to conceal what he had done.
Then Nathan the prophet confronted him.
And Nathan declared:
“Thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house…”
Then came these chilling words:
“For thou didst it secretly: but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun.”
—2 Samuel 12:11–12, KJV
Read that again.
David sinned secretly.
Years later, disgrace erupted publicly from inside his own household.
The biblical narrative itself connects these events.
What happened on Absalom’s rooftop echoes Nathan’s judgment with frightening precision.
David had hidden sexual sin.
Now sexual humiliation entered his family tragedy in full public view.

That does not mean Absalom was an innocent puppet with no moral responsibility. Scripture portrays him as making choices, receiving counsel, and acting. Nor does it make God the moral author of Absalom’s wickedness. The narrative holds human rebellion and divine judgment together without turning evil into righteousness.
But it does teach something our generation desperately needs to remember:
Forgiven sin can still leave consequences.
David had confessed.
When Nathan confronted him, David said:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
And Nathan answered:
“The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die.”
—2 Samuel 12:13, KJV
That is grace.
Real grace.
David's guilt was not beyond God's forgiveness.
But forgiveness did not magically erase every earthly consequence of everything David had done.
Somebody reading this needs that distinction.
Perhaps Jesus has forgiven you, but you are still rebuilding trust.
Perhaps you repented, but the consequences did not disappear the following morning.
Perhaps God restored your fellowship with Him, but you still have apologies to make.
Perhaps the blood of Christ has washed your guilt, but wisdom requires boundaries because of what happened.
Perhaps you are wondering whether consequences mean God did not forgive you.
Not necessarily.
Grace is not God pretending sin never mattered.
Grace is God refusing to let sin have the final word over the repentant sinner.
And David's story proves something else.
You can love God deeply and still make devastating choices.
You can write worship songs and still need repentance.
You can defeat giants in one season and lose battles with your own desires in another.
You can know Scripture and still disobey it.
You can have a testimony and still need accountability.
You can be used by God and still desperately need the mercy of God.
That should destroy spiritual arrogance.
Because Christianity is not the story of good people standing above bad people.
Christianity is the announcement that sinners need a Savior.
David needed one.
Absalom needed one.
You need one.
I need one.
And that is where this scandal begins pointing beyond David.
Because another Son of David would eventually enter Jerusalem.
But He would be nothing like Absalom.
Absalom entered Jerusalem grasping for his father’s throne.
Jesus entered Jerusalem knowing He was going toward a cross.
Absalom used people to strengthen his claim to power.
Jesus laid down His life to rescue sinners.
Absalom publicly humiliated his father.
Jesus publicly honored His Father.
Absalom sought a kingdom through rebellion.
Jesus said, “Not my will, but thine, be done.”
Absalom wanted the crown without submission.
Jesus accepted thorns before glory.
And this is the difference between the rebel son and the obedient Son.
Absalom climbed upward by violating others.
Jesus came downward to save others.
The eternal Son “made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant,” and humbled Himself “unto death, even the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:7–8).
Think about that.
The true King did not need to steal a throne.
The throne already belonged to Him.
Yet He came for rebels.
People like David.
People like us.
People who have taken God's gifts and used them against the Giver.
People who have wanted God's blessings while resisting God's authority.
People who know how to hide.
People who have made promises to God and broken them.
People whose private search history would embarrass them.
People carrying sexual shame.
People carrying adultery.
People carrying pornography.
People carrying bitterness.
People carrying secret addictions.
People carrying memories they wish they could erase.
People who look clean in church photographs while quietly wondering whether God could still want them.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross says the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with a holy God required the death of Christ.
But the cross also declares something astonishing:
Your scandal does not have to become your final identity.
David committed terrible sin, but Scripture does not end his story at Bathsheba.
Peter denied Jesus, but Scripture does not end his story beside the charcoal fire of denial.
Paul persecuted the church, but Scripture does not end his story holding the coats of those who killed Stephen.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left to repair his reputation, yet Jesus could still say, “Today shalt thou be with me in paradise.”
This is what grace does.
Grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace enters the darkness and brings the sinner into the light.
Grace does not say, “Nothing happened.”
Grace says, “Something terrible happened—and Jesus is greater.”
Grace does not remove repentance.
Grace produces it.
Grace does not teach us to excuse rebellion.
Grace brings rebels home.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe it is private.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe people still mention what you did.
Maybe your marriage carries scars.
Maybe your children remember things you wish they could forget.
Maybe you damaged someone's trust.
Maybe someone damaged yours.
Maybe you are not David in this story.
Maybe you feel like one of the people who suffered because someone powerful chose sin.
And if that is you, hear this carefully: another person's sin against you is not proof that God abandoned you.
Jesus sees wounded people too.

The women in 2 Samuel 16 were not props. They were human beings caught inside the devastation of male ambition, family collapse, and political rebellion. The later text records the painful consequences that continued in their lives.
Scripture is brutally honest about what sin does to people.
That honesty matters.
Because some wounds cannot be healed by pretending they never happened.
Christ does not ask you to call evil good.
He asks you to bring your wounds to the One who was wounded.
He was betrayed.
Publicly humiliated.
Stripped.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Condemned.
And crucified.
Jesus understands shame from the inside of human suffering.
Yet shame did not defeat Him.
Death did not defeat Him.
The grave did not keep Him.
And if you belong to Him, your darkest chapter does not get permission to write the final sentence.
That belongs to Jesus.
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Not because you needed another shocking Bible story.
Because somewhere underneath your smile, your work, your family photographs, your church attendance, your jokes, your scrolling, and your “I'm fine”…
there is something you are tired of hiding.
Then stop running toward the rooftop.
Run toward the cross.
You do not need to make yourself clean enough to approach Jesus.
Come confessing.
Come surrendering.
Come without excuses.
Come without blaming everybody else.
Come without editing the story so you look better.
Call sin what God calls it.
And trust the Christ who died for sinners.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
Not some unrighteousness.
“All unrighteousness.”
That does not make repentance cheap.
It makes Christ precious.
And maybe the most dangerous person reading this is not the person crying over obvious failure.
Maybe it is the person thinking, “At least I have never done anything like Absalom.”
Be careful.
The seed of rebellion is not measured by how spectacularly it becomes visible.
You can rebel against God quietly.
Respectably.
Religiously.
You can sit in church while protecting your throne.
You can sing “I surrender all” while mentally adding, “except that.”
You can post Scripture and refuse reconciliation.
You can preach purity while feeding secret lust.
You can talk about grace while refusing to forgive.
You can defend biblical truth while ignoring the truth about yourself.
So don't merely ask:
“How could Absalom do that?”
Ask:
“Jesus, where am I resisting You?”
That question can change a life.
Be real.
Your honesty may become the permission someone else needed to stop pretending.
Return to it when hidden compromise starts trying to sound harmless again.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
Share it with the person who thinks their past has permanently disqualified them from the mercy of Christ.
Salvation is by grace, and Christian giving and support are responses of love, not payments for blessing.
But before you leave, remember the rooftop.
Remember David.
Remember Absalom.
Remember the terrible distance sin can travel once the human heart decides God's throne belongs to us.
Then remember another hill.
Not a palace roof in Jerusalem where a rebellious son publicly declared war against his father.
A hill outside Jerusalem where the obedient Son stretched out His hands to reconcile rebels to His Father.
One rooftop displayed the ugliness of human rebellion.
One cross displayed the staggering cost of divine mercy.

And when Satan whispers that what you did is too filthy, too public, too secret, too sexual, too shameful, too hypocritical, too complicated, or simply too late for redemption, point him toward the empty tomb.
Because the Gospel has never been the story of sinners becoming impressive enough for Jesus.
It is the story of Jesus being powerful enough to save sinners.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your life—but surrender it to Christ, and it does not get to write your ending.
